newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu's fate in hands of Israel's top laywer.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu's fate in hands of Israel's top laywer.

text.p: Elyakim Rubinstein has a big decision to make.

The Israeli attorney-general appointed in the wake of a government corruption scandal in January and touted as an official without a blemish must decide if Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will stay in office or stand trial.

Rubinstein, a 49-year-old career civil servant with the unique distinction of having served as cabinet secretary in both right-wing and left-wing governments, received a police recommendation this week to indict Netanyahu and three other top officials.
Legal experts say a decision to charge the prime minister would force Netanyahu to resign and prompt new elections. State prosecutors have promised a decision within days.
"I believe he will add a lot of honour and a lot of accountability to the judicial system in Israel," Netanyahu said in January upon appointing Rubinstein.
But the man hailed as "Mr Clean" was not his first choice.
Netanyahu's appointment of fellow Likud party activist Roni Bar-On sparked a political outcry which forced Bar-On to resign 12 hours later.
A television report alleging the appointment was part of a plan to win a plea-bargain for key coalition legislator Aryeh Deri, already on trial for corruption, prompted a police probe.

Their 995-page report -- which points to Netanyahu, his director-general, Avigdor Lieberman, Justice Minister Tzachi Hanegbi and Deri -- landed on Rubinstein's desk on Tuesday. Police confirmed on Wednesday they included a rocommendation to charge Netanyahu.

Rubinstein made history in Madrid in 1991 as chief negotiator at Israel's first peace talks with Jordan and the Palestinians. Extending a hand to the Jordanians under the glare of television lights, Rubinstein addressed them as "my friends".
He has won praise from politicians across the political spectrum.
Opposition leader Shimon Peres of the Labour party, asked what he could say about Rubinstein, told Israel Radio: "Only good things. He is an extraordinarily intelligent guy."
A Tel Aviv-born religious Jew known for his quick wit and extraordinary memory, Rubinstein was hailed by Israeli newspapers at the time of his appointment as a wonder boy and man of consensus.
"With Rubinstein there will be no legal deals under the table -- everything will be according to the law and its spirit," wrote correspondent Tova Tsimuki in the newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth.
From 1977-81 Rubinstein was a key adviser to Likud foreign ministers Moshe Dayan and Yitzhak Shamir. He took part in peace talks with Egypt, including at Camp David.
In 1985-86 he served as deputy chief of mission at Israel's Washington embassy.

Appointed cabinet secretary in Likud Prime Minister Shamir's government in November 1986, Rubinstein remained on the job under Labour's Yitzhak Rabin from July 1992 until May 1994. Later he became a Jerusalem district court judge.
